about.label: About
about.heading: What is Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine)?
about.lead: A four-faced Brahma shrine in central Bangkok believed to answer prayers for career, love, health and study
about.paragraph1: Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine) stands at the corner of Ratchadamri and Phloen Chit roads, Pathum Wan, opposite CentralWorld and the Grand Hyatt Erawan. It was built in 1956 during the construction of the Erawan Hotel to dispel misfortunes that struck the project.
about.paragraph2: The Brahma image is plaster over a wooden core, gilded in gold. The four faces represent creation, prosperity, protection and benevolence. Today it is one of Thailand's most famous sacred sites, free to visit daily 06:00–22:00.

rituals.label: Worship
rituals.heading: Worship customs & offerings
rituals.quote: With a focused mind and sincere faith, what you truly wish for shall come to pass
rituals.intro: Worship at Thao Maha Brahma follows long-standing traditions — the offerings, the clockwise walk and the dance troupes all carry meaning. Here is a basic guide for first-time visitors.

steps.title: Light 3 incense, joss powder, 1 pair of candles
steps.desc: Buy offerings at the stall, light 3 incense sticks with joss powder and candles, and calm your mind

steps.title: Walk clockwise around the shrine
steps.desc: Circle the shrine to the right (clockwise) and pause to pray at each face respectfully

steps.title: Pray at each face
steps.desc: Each face represents a different blessing; make a separate wish at each one

steps.title: Hire a dance troupe (when granted)
steps.desc: When a wish is fulfilled, devotees hire a dance troupe to perform as an act of gratitude

offerings.title: Flowers (jasmine, ylang, rose)
offerings.desc: Fragrant flowers are the basic sacred offering, often made into garlands

offerings.title: Incense, candles & joss powder
offerings.desc: 3 incense sticks and a candle pair are used for prayer; joss powder is sprinkled

offerings.title: Fruit & ceremonial items
offerings.desc: Seasonal fruit and other items are placed on the offering table

offerings.title: Red cloth & donations
offerings.desc: Red cloth and donations are commonly offered for good fortune

rituals.dance: Dance troupes are hired to perform for the deity. When a wish is granted, devotees return to hire a troupe in gratitude. Some troupes have dozens of performers and several perform together in the evening, creating a beautiful and festive atmosphere.

history.label: History
history.heading: History & legends of Thao Maha Brahma (Erawan Shrine)
history.intro: From Hindu deity worship absorbed into Thai Brahmin rituals, this shrine grew from a small corner into a symbol of Bangkok

blocks.title: Origins (1956)
blocks.text: During construction of the Erawan Hotel several fatal accidents occurred. A Brahmin priest was consulted and a Brahma shrine was built in front of the hotel for good fortune; the misfortunes then ceased.

blocks.title: The four-faced belief
blocks.text: The four faces represent creation, long life, prosperity and protection. Worshippers walk clockwise and pray at each face in turn.

blocks.title: The 1994 incident
blocks.text: A mentally ill man smashed the image with a hammer; an angry crowd killed him. The original was preserved in a museum and a replica was made.

blocks.title: The current image
blocks.text: After a 2006 attack, a new bronze-and-gold image replaced the plaster one for durability, and it remains open for worship to this day.

legend.title: The legend of its sacredness
legend.text: It is said that those who pray with sincere faith and have their wishes granted often return to give thanks with dance troupes. This belief made the shrine one of Asia's most famous wish-making sites, especially among visitors from China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan.

didYouKnow.title: Did you know?
didYouKnow.text: Although Brahma is a Hindu deity, the shrine is maintained by Thai Brahmin ritual and is revered equally by Buddhists and Hindus.

folklore.title: Tales from the elders
folklore.tale: It is said Brahma is the creator god, so people offer flowers, scents and dance to show gratitude.
folklore.shrine: When life succeeds, they speak of the merit made at this shrine, and return to pray again and again.

faqs.q: What time does Erawan Shrine close?
faqs.a: The shrine opens at 06:00 and closes at 22:00 every day, including public holidays. The last thanks-giving dance round stops taking bookings about 30 minutes before closing.

faqs.q: How much does a thanks-giving dance troupe cost?
faqs.a: Official foundation rates: 260 baht for 2 dancers, 360 baht for 4, 460 baht for 6 and 710 baht for 8, per performance. Book at the desk inside the shrine grounds only — outside troupes are not accepted.
The shrine is operated by the Than Tao Mahaprom Foundation (มูลนิธิทุนท่านท้าวมหาพรหม), which runs the official offering stalls and the dance troupe booking desk inside the fenced area.

faqs.q: Where can I find official information about the shrine?
faqs.a: The shrine is managed by the Than Tao Mahaprom Foundation; official tourism information about the site and district is published by the Tourism Authority of Thailand.

knowledge.title: Background: Phra Phrom vs Indra
knowledge.text: Phra Phrom (Brahma) is the creator god and the main image of this shrine; Indra rules the Trayastrimsa heaven and is a guardian deity who averts misfortune. The Ratchaprasong intersection is a sacred zone watched over by eight Hindu deities, and the Indra shrine in front of Amarin Plaza stands barely a hundred metres from the Erawan Shrine. That is why the on-site notice board also carries chants honouring and petitioning Indra — a sign of how inclusively these beliefs are blended.

chant.label: Chants
chant.heading: The Phra Phrom katha and opening invocation
chant.intro: The shrine's official texts are short katha — all of them fit on one screen and can be chanted standing up. Pick whichever suits you: the short form if you are in a hurry, the full katha if you want to do it properly.
chant.note: These chants are Thai phonetic renderings of Sanskrit and Pali, and spellings differ slightly between sources (for example พรหมเรสสะยัม and พรหมเวสสะยัม) without changing the sound. Sincere focus matters more than exact wording, so do not worry about mispronouncing.

blocks.title: 1. Opening invocation: the triple homage (Namo Tassa)
blocks.desc: The standard opening homage in Thai Buddhist and Brahmin rites, recited before any request.
blocks.thai: นะโม ตัสสะ ภะคะวะโต อะระหะโต สัมมา สัมพุทธัสสะ
blocks.roman: Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammā Sambuddhassa
blocks.pronunciation: NA-mo TAS-sa pa-ka-wa-to a-ra-ha-to SAM-ma sam-put-TAS-sa
blocks.meaning: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One.

blocks.title: 2. Main chant: the Phra Phrom katha (โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม)
blocks.desc: The most widely circulated official katha for the Erawan shrine. Reading all twelve lines once counts as one round.

lines.thai: โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม
โองการะ นิสสะวะรัง
พรหมเรสสะยัม ภูปัสสะวะวิษณุ
ไวยะทานะโมโทติ
ลูกะปัม ทะระมา ยิกยานัง
ยะไวยะลา คะมุลัม สะทา
นันตะระ วิมุสะตินัน
นะมัตเต นะมัตเตเร
จะ อะการัง ตโถวาจะ
เอตามา ตาระยัต ตะมัน ตะรามา
กัตถะ นารัมลา จะสะระวะ ปะติตัม
สัมโภ พะกลโล ทิวะทิยัม มะตัมยะ

blocks.pronunciationNote: Thai is a tonal language and the Roman line is the reliable reading aid. As an orientation, the opening line โอมปะระเมสะ นะมัสสะการัม sounds roughly like "ohm pa-ra-ME-sa na-MAT-sa-ka-ram".
blocks.meaning: This is an act of homage and refuge to Brahma: it opens with โอม (Om), the primordial sound, followed by นะมัสสะการัม, "I bow in reverence", and continues as a request for blessing, protection and grace. Because the whole text is a Thai phonetic rendering of Sanskrit, a reliable word-by-word translation has been lost in transmission; the accepted sense is simply an earnest homage to Brahma asking for blessing and protection.

blocks.title: 3. Short form: the Phra Phrom heart mantra (โอม พรหมมายะ นะมะห์)
blocks.desc: A single line — useful when you are short of time or cannot linger in the crowd.
blocks.thai: โอม พรหมมายะ นะมะห์

faces.label: Worship order
faces.heading: Four faces clockwise — what to ask at each
faces.intro: Start with the face you find yourself looking at as you enter, then move clockwise. The order should not be reversed, and you should never walk against it.

items.desc: Job hunting, promotion, exams, starting a business — direction and prospects
Partnership, family harmony and helpful people around you

Your body, your family's wellbeing and clearing bad luck

faces.tip: The four-face attributions are folk tradition and vary between communities. If you already follow a set order, pray in the way you know with a sincere mind — what matters is covering all four faces, not just one.

steps.label: Step by step
steps.heading: How to worship on site: six steps
steps.intro: From buying incense to returning a vow — follow these the first time you go.

items.title: Buy your offerings at the foundation stall inside the fence
items.desc: 12 incense sticks, 4 garlands and 1 candle, with prices clearly displayed. Do not buy from roaming vendors outside the fence.

items.title: Wash your hands, settle your mind, chant the homage three times
items.desc: Recite Namo Tassa three times and let your mind quieten before making a wish — devotees consider focus far more important than expensive offerings.

items.title: Start at the front face and go clockwise
items.desc: At each face place 3 incense sticks and 1 garland, put your palms together and state your name, date of birth and your wish.

items.title: Place the candle on the face you care most about
items.desc: There is only one candle, so put it on the face that matters most for this visit. Under current rules incense and candles are not lit.

items.title: Return to the front face and chant the main katha
items.desc: Walk back round to the first face, chant the katha 3 times (or 9), bow with palms together and you are done.

items.title: Come back to give thanks when the wish is granted
items.desc: Devotees believe a promise made must be kept. See "Offerings & vows" below for the options.

offerings.label: Offerings & vows
offerings.heading: Offering set and how to return a vow

set.note: Placed on the face you care most about. Some stalls sell sets with 4 candles — one per face is also acceptable

offerings.elephantNote: Wooden elephants are the most common thanks-offering, and the larger the size the greater the thanks. Buy them at the foundation stall inside the fence; sizes over 40 inches are not accepted.
offerings.danceTitle: Thanks-giving dance (ละครชาตรี)
offerings.danceNote: Hiring a dance troupe once your wish is granted is the shrine's most famous form of thanks. Rates are set and posted by the foundation, and bookings must be made inside the shrine — outside private troupes are not accepted.
offerings.danceFlow: The person giving thanks kneels in front of the troupe, the lead dancer announces their name and what was granted, and the dancers perform to traditional Pi Phat music. Each round lasts under 15 minutes.

taboos.label: Etiquette
taboos.heading: What not to do at the shrine

items.title: Incense and candles are never lit
items.desc: Under the city and foundation smoke-free initiative, offerings may be placed but not lit.

items.title: Do not release birds you brought yourself
items.desc: This is an explicit current rule, with a 500 baht fine for violations.

items.title: Walk clockwise, never against the flow
items.desc: Going anticlockwise is considered disrespectful and blocks other worshippers.

items.title: Dress modestly and remove your hat to pray
items.desc: Less strict than a temple, but avoid very revealing clothing.

items.title: Do not pose with your back to the image
items.desc: Folk belief holds that turning your back on the image is disrespectful. Also avoid photographing people mid-prayer.

items.title: Folk custom: avoid beef before worshipping
items.desc: This circulates among devotees and is not an official rule. If it matters to you, skip beef the day before.

items.title: Wishes should be fair and harm no one
items.desc: Devotees widely hold that a request that profits by harming others will not be answered.

items.title: Keep the promise you made
items.desc: Whatever form of thanks you promised while wishing must be carried out — this is the single most important principle here.

faqs.q: How many times should I chant the Erawan Shrine prayer?
faqs.a: Recite the Namo Tassa homage 3 times, the main Phra Phrom katha 3 or 9 times, and the short heart mantra 4 times. If you are short of time, four rounds of the short mantra is enough — focus matters more than the count.

faqs.q: Can I chant if I do not speak Thai?
faqs.a: Yes. The text is a Thai phonetic rendering of Sanskrit and Pali, so simply follow the Roman transliteration. Devotees generally hold that sincerity and focus matter more than perfect pronunciation.

faqs.q: What should I pray for at each of the four faces?
faqs.a: Starting from the face you meet as you enter and going clockwise: career and study, then love and relationships, then wealth, then health and safety. These attributions are folk tradition and vary between communities, so simply make sure you cover all four faces.

faqs.q: Do I have to come back and give thanks?
faqs.a: In the prevailing belief, yes — the form of thanks you promised while making the wish must be carried out. Common options are a wooden elephant, hiring a dance troupe, or a donation, depending on how big the wish was and what you can afford.

faqs.q: How long does a prayer visit take?
faqs.a: Around 15 to 30 minutes for the worship itself. In the evening, when thanks-giving troupes perform back to back, expect to stay longer and to find it more crowded.

faqs.q: Are the offerings sold on site a rip-off?
faqs.a: The foundation stalls inside the fence display fixed prices and are the safe place to buy. Vendors outside the fence often sell the same set at several times the price — do not buy from them.
